points.title: Le subjonctif : révision et liste des déclencheurs
points.explanationEn:
This is the capstone grammar point of the B1 level, pulling together everything you've learned about the subjonctif présent — formation, the necessity trigger il faut que, and the opinion/will/doubt triggers — into one organized reference, plus one final category you haven't formally covered yet: emotion. By now you should recognize the core mechanic: the subjunctive appears in a que-clause whenever the main clause frames that clause as something other than a plain, certain fact — a wish, a requirement, a doubt, a judgment, or, as you'll now add, a feeling.

The new category is émotion: verbs and expressions of feeling — being happy, sad, surprised, afraid, angry, or relieved about something — trigger the subjunctive in the clause that describes what's causing the feeling, because emotional reactions are inherently subjective, not neutral fact. Je suis content que tu sois là (I'm happy that you're here), Elle est triste que son ami parte (She's sad that her friend is leaving), Nous avons peur qu'il pleuve (We're afraid it will rain), Ça m'étonne qu'elle n'ait pas répondu (It surprises me that she hasn't answered). Just like with vouloir que, the subjunctive here only appears when the subject of the emotion is different from the subject of the thing felt about — if the subject stays the same, French switches to an infinitive construction instead: Je suis content d'être là (I'm happy to be here — no que, no subjunctive, because 'I' am both content and there).

Putting it all together, here is the working reference list of subjunctive triggers by category. Volonté/necessité (will/necessity): vouloir que, souhaiter que, préférer que, il faut que, il est nécessaire que, il est essentiel que. Doute/possibilité (doubt/possibility): douter que, il est possible que, il n'est pas certain que, ne pas penser/croire que (negated only). Jugement/opinion (impersonal value judgment): il est important que, il est dommage que, il vaut mieux que, il est bizarre/étonnant que. Émotion (feeling): être content/heureux/triste/surpris/désolé que, avoir peur que, regretter que, craindre que. As a working test you can apply to any new expression you meet: try substituting 'is this presenting the following clause as an objective fact, or as something wanted, doubted, judged, or felt?' If it's a plain fact, use the indicative (il est vrai que, je sais que, il est certain que all take the indicative, since they assert certainty rather than subjectivity). If it falls into one of the four subjective categories above, use the subjunctive.

Finally, remember the two structural constants that hold across every trigger: (1) the subjunctive only appears after que introducing a clause with its own (usually different) subject — same-subject sentences drop que and use an infinitive instead; and (2) nous/vous forms of stem-changing verbs use the imparfait-style stem while je/tu/il/ils use the ils-present stem (que je vienne but que nous venions), a pattern that holds for every single verb in every trigger category, with only être, avoir, aller, faire, savoir, vouloir, pouvoir, and falloir needing to be memorized as fully irregular exceptions to that otherwise fully predictable system.

examples.fr: Je suis content que tu sois venu à mon anniversaire.
examples.en: I'm happy that you came to my birthday.

examples.fr: Je suis content d'être venu à ton anniversaire.
examples.en: I'm happy that I came to your birthday.
examples.note: Same subject → infinitive, no que, no subjunctive.

examples.fr: Elle a peur que son couple ne dure pas.
examples.en: She's afraid her relationship won't last.

examples.fr: Nous voulons que vous soyez heureux ensemble.
examples.en: We want you to be happy together.

examples.fr: Il est essentiel que les amis se disent la vérité.
examples.en: It's essential that friends tell each other the truth.

examples.fr: Je doute qu'il soit vraiment amoureux d'elle.
examples.en: I doubt he's really in love with her.

examples.fr: C'est dommage que vous ne puissiez pas venir au mariage.
examples.en: It's a shame you can't come to the wedding.

examples.fr: Il est vrai que l'amitié demande des efforts.
examples.en: It's true that friendship takes effort.
examples.note: Certainty trigger (il est vrai que) → indicative, NOT subjunctive.

examples.fr: Nous regrettons que tu ne nous aies rien dit plus tôt.
examples.en: We regret that you didn't tell us anything sooner.
examples.note: Emotion trigger (regretter que), subjunctive past (aies dit).

examples.fr: Il faut que nous soyons honnêtes l'un envers l'autre.
examples.en: We need to be honest with each other.
examples.note: Nécessité trigger (il faut que), reciprocal l'un envers l'autre.

commonMistakes: Using an infinitive after an emotion verb even when the subjects differ, by analogy with the same-subject case (writing 'je suis content tu viennes' or 'je suis content que tu viens' instead of 'je suis content que tu sois venu').
Applying the subjunctive to certainty expressions like il est vrai que, il est certain que, or je sais que, which take the indicative because they assert fact rather than subjectivity.
Forgetting that negating a certainty verb (ne pas savoir que, ne pas être sûr que) flips it into subjunctive territory, while leaving it unnegated correctly stays indicative.

Mixing up the two subjunctive stems for stem-changing verbs across different trigger categories, not just with il faut que (e.g. getting 'que nous venions' right after il faut que but wrong after je suis content que).
Treating the subjunctive as a fixed list of memorized phrases rather than an underlying logic, and therefore failing to apply it correctly to a new, previously unseen trigger expression.
whyItTrips: By B1 capstone level, learners have absorbed several subjunctive triggers in isolation across earlier units but have rarely had to sort a mixed batch of them on the fly — recognizing which of four categories (will, doubt, judgment, emotion) an unfamiliar expression belongs to, in real time, is a harder skill than recalling one memorized phrase.

English marks emotional reactions with the same flat indicative-style grammar it uses for everything else ('I'm happy that you came' looks structurally identical to 'I know that you came'), so English gives no grammatical signal that emotion clauses need special treatment the way French does.

The subjunctive/indicative boundary is genuinely a semantic judgment (is this fact or subjectivity?) rather than a mechanical rule, so building reliable, fast intuition for it requires much more exposure and practice than form-based rules like verb conjugation endings.
